newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian firms on warpath over Prodi's budget plans.
newsitem.headline: Italian firms on warpath over Prodi's budget plans.

text.p: The Italian government, desperate for cash in the race towards EMU, looks set to dip into huge reservoirs of company severance payment funds despite bitter opposition from the business world.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi is due to unveil a mini-budget by the end of the week, which is expected to include 16 trillion lire ($9.5 billion) of deficit cutting initiatives in a bid to prepare the economy for the single European currency.
Treasury sources said between 6.0-7.0 trillion lire of this should come from an enforced transfer of severance payment funds, with only smaller firms being spared from the measure.
Industrialists have warned of serious consequencies if these funds, which are regularly used as a cheap source of self-financing, are depleted.

Business federation Confindustria has described the plan as "predatory" while the chairman of car group Fiat warned that if Prodi presses ahead with the plan, tensions would rise between the industrial and political classes.

"I call on ministers to reflect very, very hard on this," Cesare Romiti said. Newspapers have speculated that Fiat alone might see over 500 billion lire sucked from its balance sheet if the measure was introduced. Fiat declined to comment.
The funds were set up in the 1920s as a way of financing pension needs, with a portion of employees' salaries held in reserve to be handed over as a lump sum when they retire.
Analysts estimate that Italian companies now hold some 185 trillion lire in severance payments.

Economists said they understood companies' anguish, with firms facing the prospect of having to draw expensive bank loans if their severance reserves are capped, but added that whatever happened, the funds looked doomed to wither.

"Obviously company costs will increase unless there is some sort of compensation," said Giovanna Mossetti, chief economist with Milan brokers Caboto. "But who is going to stop the government taking these funds away?"

Plundering these funds is an enormously attractive option for the centre-left government, which is eager not to hurt voters with more tax hikes and is not politically strong enough to force through cutbacks in the generous state pensions system.

In addition, although the measure will simply create future liabilities for Rome, it will boost coffers in the short-term and will almost certainly be approved by Brussels as a valid way of reducing the public administration deficit.

The Treasury already took two trillion lire from the funds in the 1997 budget in the form of early tax demands, while France pulled off a similar accounting sleight of hand last year, adding 37.5 billion francs ($6.6 billion) to accounts via a special transfer of pension funds from France Telecom.
But with the state's pension liabilities already seen as too large, analysts question how wise it would be for the government to take over big chunks of the severance payments.

The Treasury had indicated that it wanted to divert the funds into the small private pension sector and some dailies have suggested that the government might exempt companies from the forthcoming transfer if they sign up to the pension schemes.

"That would be very welcome news for private pensions, but I don't think the sector is developed enough for that kind of incentive yet," said a London analyst who declined to be named. "(But) in the end these severance funds look certain to be taken from companies in one way or another," he added.
